title: Immune Cells in Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias in the Jackson Heart Study
text: Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD) are a major cause of morbidity and mortality (6th leading cause of death in the United States). African American adults are at high risk, and chronic inflammation may be a key biological risk factor. The proposed work will assess specific innate and adaptive immune cells, and genes expressed in these cells, and determine whether they are associated with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and dementia risk among African Americans from the population-based Jackson Heart Study, as well as target genes and biological mechanisms in immune cells for genetic variants previously associated with dementia.

title: Characterizing the role of affective information in early word learning using observational and experimental designs
text:
The goal of this project is to develop and test a framework describing the multimodal affective environment
that supports language development in early childhood. Using computational analyses of infants’ at-home
environments in the first years of life as well as a series of tightly-controlled experiments, we ask (1) how
affective contexts shape word learning and (2) how children with depressed caregivers adapt their learning
strategies to the decreased affective information in their environments. Understanding how children with
depressed caregivers use affective information to learn new words may inform tailored efforts to promote
equity in educational outcomes.

title: Urine based circulating tumor DNA analysis
text:
Our long-term goal is to establish 24-hour urine-based ctDNA testing as an effective liquid biopsy alternative to
blood-based approaches for non-genitourinary cancers. Our preliminary data demonstrates that a 24-hour
urine-based HPV DNA and ctDNA analysis approach using phased variants is more sensitive than blood-based
testing. We will validate our urine-based analytical approach and determine if it detects more HPV DNA and
ctDNA phased variants than matched blood tests in patients with early-stage oropharyngeal cancer and in an
in vivo xenograft model.

title: Dissecting the tumor-intrinsic and -extrinsic roles of TBK1 in tumor immunity
text:
Melanoma is the fifth most common form of cancer in adults (men and women) and is the
deadliest form of skin cancer (NCI-SEER-Database, 2019), and has been rising in the
United States and worldwide (Karimkhani et al., 2017; Schadendorf et al., 2018), with an
estimated 96,480 adults (57,220 men and 39,260 women) diagnosed with melanoma in
the United States in 2019, accounting for 5.5% of all new cancer cases and resulting in
7,230 deaths (1.2% of all cancer deaths). While the treatment of metastatic melanoma
has undergone a dramatic transformation over the past decade with the advent of
molecular targeted therapy and immunotherapy, additional therapeutic approaches are
needed for patients resistant to available targeted and immune treatments. We have
identified TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1) is an emerging target to overcome resistance to
cancer immunotherapy and aim to define the cell type specific roles of TBK1 in tumor
immunity.

title: PIPELINE Facility Core
text: PIPELINE FACILITY CORE The Vision for the PIPELINE (Promoting Impact of Precision EHS by Leveraging Instrumentation, NextGen and Emerging Technologies) Core is to provide access to expertise and technologies, and facilitate effective utilization of “omic” technologies across the parent organizations of the Gulf Coast Center for Precision Environmental Health (GC-CPEH) to advance environmental health science (EHS) research. The PIPELINE Facility Core provides efficient systems level access, enabling researchers from all Thematic Focus Areas to incorporate multiple NextGen “omics” technologies into their research. PIPELINE provides services in 1) Genomics, Epigenomics and Transcriptomics, 2) Proteomics, 3) Metabolomics, 4) Microbiome and Metagenomics, 5) Cells-to-Tissues-to-Organisms, and 6) MultiOmic Data Analysis. To support utilization, the PIPELINE Facility Core 1) provides consultation to Center members to identify the best state-of-the-art technologies to meet their research goals; 2) works with members to ensure efficient project design and comprehensive data generation; 3) delivers individualized training, and develops workshops and Resource Educational Sessions; and, 4) provides robust bioinformatic analyses and data interpretation integrating multiple platforms to ultimately provide systems-level knowledge. Importantly, resource access and utilization are facilitated by subject-matter experts serving as Resource Navigators for GC-CPEH members. Resource Navigators provide expertise, prioritize access, and assist members with project design, data generation and bioinformatics analyses. This Core also supports the educational and mentoring needs of members through individualized training, seminars, workshops, and participation in the Leadership Development Program of the Center’s Career Development Program. Access and utilization of PIPELINE services are facilitated via a Matching Funds Core Utilization Program, which significantly reduces the cost of services. The following Specific Aims are designed to ensure the PIPELINE Facility Core achieves the goal of advancing EHS research for GC-CPEH investigators and via cross-Center collaborations, EHS researchers at other EHS Core Centers. Specific Aim 1: Provide high-quality, user-friendly NextGen resources to accelerate precision environmental health research and increase the impact of GC-CPEH research; Specific Aim 2: Contribute to the career development of promising new investigators and enable utilization of new technologies by senior investigators; and Specific Aim 3: Increase the impact of the GC-CPEH research base by integrating across Center components and institutions and contributing to exploratory Pilot Project research and high-impact publications.

title: Polarity Signals Coordinate Neuronal Differentiation & Nuclear Organization
text:
During neural development, the maturation of nerve cells drives fundamental cellular processes that
assemble neuronal circuitry. This proposal studies the mechanisms governing the cell biology of neuronal
differentiation and how developing neurons organize their chromatin during this process. The imaging
tools and conceptual advances developed by this proposal will not only expand our knowledge of neural
development but could lead to new diagnostics and treatments for neurodevelopmental disorders, such
as pediatric cancers or developmental defects associated with pre-term birth.

title: Molecular Regulation of Radial Intercalation
text:
Relevance:
The ability of cells to migrate through junctional barriers is important during tissue morphogenesis, tissue
homeostasis and during cancer metastasis. The goal of this project is to understand the molecular regulation of
microtubule acetylation and vertex strength during migration and intercalation in a reproducible 3 dimensional in
vivo system.

title: Modeling Metastasis and Acquired Drug Resistance Using Circulating Tumor Cells
text:
Advanced breast cancers of the most common type (Estrogen Receptor (ER) positive) initially respond
to hormonal therapy, but then become resistant to further therapy. As they invade, breast cancers shed
cells into the bloodstream (Circulating Tumor Cells; CTCs), which we have been able to culture repeatedly
in the laboratory during the course of therapy, providing an exceptional resource to better understand
acquired drug resistance. Using these patient-derived cell cultures, we propose to apply sophisticated
functional genomic and chemical proteomic technologies to characterize and ultimately overcome the
most common, and least well understood, mechanism of acquired resistance to hormonal therapy,
namely the complete loss of ER expression in breast cancers that were initially ER positive.

title: STATE-DEPENDENT MODULATION OF CEREBELLAR FUNCTION
text:
Brain states vary throughout the day, impacting performance in ways that can have life or death consequences,
e.g. driving a car while starting to nod off, or performing surgery while distracted. The experiments in this
application examine neural states associated with high- and low-performance in the cerebellum, an area of the
brain that plays a critical role in a wide range of motor and cognitive functions. The long-term goal of the
project is to develop therapeutic strategies, such as walking or non-invasive brain stimulation, that can boost
the function of the cerebellum, both in health and disease, by promoting high-performance states.

title: Durability of memory T cell responses in melanoma
text:
Resident memory T (TRM) cells are critical participants in antitumor immune responses. Their role during the
activation and generation of memory T cell responses during the growth of primary melanomas are unknown.
We will investigate the role of TRM in primary melanoma and skin in order to facilitate future clinical trials.

title: Investigation of Physical Constriction on Cancer Stem Cells
text:
Cancer stem cells (CSCs) are a small but critically important subset of cancer cells responsible for
chemoresistance, dormancy, and tumor initiation. This project will draw upon engineering and biological sciences
to study in vitro the influence of physical forces on the selection, induction, and/or sustainment of metastasizing
cancer stem cells, and evaluate their retention, survival and extravasation efficiency in the in vivo lung.
Successful completion of this project will provide new platforms for investigating the effect of physical constriction
on a variety of pathways activated during cancer metastasis, an understanding of the impact of mechanical
microenvironment on cancer stem cells, and potentially point to potential new combination therapies (with
chemotherapy) to try to combat the further spread of metastatic disease.

title: Novel Zinc-Finger Protein Regulator of Senescence and Cell Engineering
text:
Intervertebral disc disorders and back pain are linked to senescence, which contributes to back pain through the
expression of an array of molecules. We have discovered a novel protein that directly regulates this process and
has the potential to improve our understanding of back pain development and has potential to be utilized as a
novel treatment target.

title: DNASU - National Resource
text:
PROJECT RELEVANCE
The DNASU Plasmid Repository collects or create genes and other DNA-based resources, verifies that they
are correct, maintains them safely for long term storage, and distributes them worldwide at low cost to scientific
researchers to accelerate research and discovery. Sharing these plasmids will continue to provide tools to
develop a better understanding of disease and potential biomarker targets to aid in disease diagnosis and
treatment.

title: Functional Roles of Human Cytochrome P450 Enzymes
text:
Many of the chemicals that cause cancer are made either more or less active by cytochrome P450
(P450) enzymes in the body. Three enzymes are also involved in the metabolism of drugs, including those
used to treat cancer. The enzymes are also involved in the metabolism of steroids and influence hormone
action.

title: Respiring Osteoarthritis: Oxygen-Generating and Cytokine-Binding Biomaterials for Enhanced Stem Cell Activity
text:
Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint condition that remains difficult to treat with stem cell-based therapies due
to its complex disease pathology, including imbalances in oxygen supply and demand. Approaches seeking to
control oxygen levels within the joint space have seen limited translations success due to biomaterial design
challenges, such as cytotoxicity, hyperoxia, and loss of oxygen-binding protein function. The proposed studies
will here pioneer the development of sophisticated hemoglobin-based biomaterials with oxygen delivery
capabilities to enhance stem cell health and secretome activity, following intra-articular injections in vitro and in
vivo.

title: Radiotracer-Based Imaging for Quantitative Assessment of Skeletal Muscle Perfusion in Peripheral Artery Disease
text:
Lower extremity peripheral artery disease (PAD) is an atherosclerotic disease that is associated with increased
levels of arterial calcification above and below the knee, which decreases blood flow and perfusion to the calves
and feet, and increases risk of non-healing wounds, limb loss, and death. Our research team developed a novel
PET/CT imaging paradigm that provides absolute measures of skeletal muscle perfusion within specific muscle
groups and vascular territories of the lower extremities that correspond with adverse remodeling of skeletal
muscle and PAD symptom severity. The overarching goal of the outlined projects is to pre-clincially test and
clinically translate this functional imaging approach to comprehensively quantify regional abnormalities in lower
extremity skeletal muscle perfusion in the setting of PAD, which could ultimately assist the vascular medicine
community by improving non-invasive monitoring of PAD patients, evaluating the efficacy of targeted
revascularization procedures, and predicting rates of major adverse limb events after therapeutic interventions.

title: Tracking the impact of screen media activity on mental health, cognition and the brain from childhood to adolescence in the longitudinal ABCD study
text:
This project will be the largest multimodal longitudinal study in children and adolescents attempting to identify
robust neural and mental health correlates and consequences specific to three Screen Media Activity (SMA)
types: active (i.e., videogaming), passive (i.e., watching TV and videos) and mixed (i.e., texting and using social
media). Its innovation lies in the multi-modal and longitudinal characterization of the children and the use of twin-
studies and sophisticated analytic methods to identify probable causal mechanisms involving SMA types. The
rationale for the proposed research is that, once the neurobiological mechanisms mediating the relationship
among SMA, mental health and brain development are understood, and modifiable factors identified, targeted
prevention approaches and policy initiatives can be developed.

title: UCLA Tumor Immunology Institutional Training Grant
text:
Cancer remains the top killer of adults under 85 worldwide, but recent advances that unleash the power of the
immune system against tumors has shown impressive progress against many forms of intractable cancer,
necessitating the advanced training of research specialists at the interface of oncology and immunology. The
UCLA Tumor Immunology Training Program (TITP) is dedicated to mentored, interdisciplinary team-based
training of a new generation of academic and industry leaders in basic, translational, and clinical research in
tumor immunology. By deploying facilities and resources of a renowned immunotherapy trials epicenter that
includes the NCI-designated Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center and the Parker Institute for Cancer
Immunotherapy, we aim to fulfill this training mission while uncovering basic principles in host-tumor
interactions and developing next-generation therapies based in fundamental tumor immunology for the
betterment of cancer patients and their families.

title: Defining the role of Atg9b in the aging heart
text:
This research will investigate how a protein called Atg9b helps maintain healthy mitochondria and heart function
during aging. Understanding this process may reveal new ways to prevent or slow heart failure in older adults.
The findings could help identify new therapies that preserve energy production and support healthy heart function
with age.

title: Development of a Foundation Model for Live Cell Phenotyping to Transform Cancer Research and Therapy
text:
We will develop a foundation model that enables automated, high-throughput analysis of live cell imaging data
to characterize cellular morphodynamics in real-time. The resulting platform will streamline live cell
phenotyping workflows, accelerate drug discovery, and facilitate personalized treatment strategies, addressing
critical challenges in cancer research.
